chapter: Billie Holiday, Basie leadership and studio work
title: Black musicians and the studios; Lee Young on staff
summary: The best pay was in unseen recording; studios excluded black musicians except Lee Young at Columbia.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: I really couldn't tell you all the names of films. Many times, when you work in a film, the part where you make the most money is the part where you're never seen, which is the recording element of it. I guess during those days, during the early days of film recording, I was probably as much as any black guy in this vicinity here, although I was never hired as a regular on -- by any studio, because it was practically verboten. There were just no black guys out there.
That was the days of the separate , right?

That's the days in the separate locals and even -- it didn't actually get any until after both locals got together or regular. The only guy -- there was one guy that actually had a regular job out there. That was Lee Young at Columbia in the late '30s. He had a regular job, staff. He was on staff.
Don't know. He got on. They needed a good drummer and Lee did a nice job.
